newsitem.title: USA: Kasich, others attack US corporate welfare schemes.
newsitem.headline: Kasich, others attack US corporate welfare schemes.

text.p: An unusual alliance of left and right-wing groups on Tuesday unveiled a "hit list" of a dozen "corporate welfare" programs they want eliminated by the federal government.
The programs, which cost the government billions of dollars each year, range from U.S. support for International Monetary Fund activities to road construction in Appalachia.

The alliance, which includes the conservative Americans for Tax Reform and the environmental group Friends of the Earth, has the backing of House Budget Committee Chairman John Kasich from Ohio and other lawmakers.

Among the projects targetted are the Agriculture Department's market access program, which pays companies to advertise overseas; fossil energy research and development at the Energy Department, which provides grants for oil, gas, and coal research; and the clean coal technology program.

The alliance also wants to eliminate the Overseas Private Investment Corp, which provides insurance to U.S. exporters, and to cut off funding for the IMF's General Arrangements to Borrow (GAB) and its Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility.
The latter facility provides low-cost financing to the world's poorest nations.

The GAB, which the IMF on Monday voted to supplement with additional funds, is designed for use in financial emergencies that threaten the world economy. It requires authorization by Congress, but not a direct appropriation of money.
Kasich in the past has led the charge against so-called "corporate welfare" programs, but has had limited success at best in eliminating them.
In helping to put together the unusual alliance of left and right-wing groups, the Ohio Republican is hoping to garner political support for his drive.

A group of senators, led by Republican John McCairn from Arizona and Democrat Edward Kennedy from Massaceusetts, plan to introduce a bill to create an independent commission to review government subsidies and tax breaks for businesses.
The commission would be modelled along the lines of the panel set up by Congress to shut down military bases -- another politically difficult issue fro lawmakers.

The Taxpayers for Common Sense, which is one of the members of the alliance against corporate welfare, called the group an "odd couple coalition" of taxpayer, environmental, consumer and free market organizations.
It said the hit list signals out 12 programs for large savings over the next five years or the life of the program:
- the Rural Utility Service Electricity and Telephone Loan Program, $190 million,
- the Market Access Program, $347 million to help U.S. exporters, including Hershey Food Corp and Campbell Soup, to promote their products overseas,
- the Animas-La Plata Project, $432 million to irrigate farms,
- the Pyroprocessing Program, $100 million to reprocess nuclear fuel,
- the Appalachian Regional Commission Road Program, $500 million for highway construction,
- the Fossil Energy Research and Development Program, $1.37 billion in the first year for applied energy technologies,
- timber road building in national forests, $100 million to rebate timber companies for cutting new roads,
- the Clean Coal Technology Program, $500 million for pollution abatement technologies,
- the Overseas Private Investment Corp, $281 million to insure U.S. investments overseas,
- the IMF's GAB, $3.5 billion,
- the IMF's Enhanced Structural Adjustment Facility, $150 million,
- and highway demonstration projects, $4 billion for roads.
